profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research group preparing the next two-week sprint for a paper and internal demo on reinforcement-learning-based induction machine design. The team already has an offline-trained RL agent that proposes motor geometry and winding parameters from customer requirements, and they now need to plan the work needed to turn the current prototype into a credible research artifact for a sales-tool-facing demo. The agenda is to decide what counts as the upcoming 'planner' deliverable, what evaluation package will be assembled, how the simulation loop will be run for the next training batch, and who will own integration tasks. The expected outcome is a division of responsibilities and a timeline for producing a demoable planner, refreshed training results, and a short internal report for the lab lead.

members.name: Dr. Lena Hoffmann
members.expertise: Reinforcement learning for engineering design, surrogate-model-based optimization, experimental evaluation
members.background: Lena joined the lab after a PhD in applied machine learning for industrial design automation and currently leads the learning-system side of the motor-design project.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, publishable planning story with stable experimental evidence and is worried that too much engineering integration work will consume the sprint without improving the paper.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'planner', it means the RL policy plus the lightweight normalization and constraint-check wrapper used in offline experiments, not a production-facing quotation component.
A 'validated' design means it passes the lab's fast electromagnetic-thermal screening thresholds over the held-out requirement set, even if no designer reviews individual machine proposals.

Running the next training batch on the 'full simulator' still means the existing hybrid loop with cached finite-element outcomes and surrogate thermal estimates, because that is the standard setup in the research codebase.
The handoff on Friday means end of day in Munich with materials ready for internal review, not necessarily packaged for another team to directly invoke.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Model deployment, optimization pipelines, simulation infrastructure, tool integration
members.background: Arjun previously worked on engineering software platforms and now translates research prototypes into internal tools that other teams can call from sales and design workflows.
members.private_state: He wants the sprint to produce something operational enough that the sales-tool team can try it immediately, and he is concerned that another purely research-oriented cycle will not reduce downstream integration risk.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'planner', it means a callable service endpoint that takes customer specs and returns a ranked machine proposal package suitable for quotation workflows.
A 'validated' design means at least a few output designs have been checked by a motor designer or high-fidelity simulation so downstream users can trust the recommendations.
The 'full simulator' refers to running fresh multiphysics evaluations for each new candidate in this sprint's batch rather than leaning mainly on prior cached results.
A Friday handoff means a usable artifact committed and documented by Friday so the consuming team can start testing the same day.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to deliver 'the planner' by the end of the sprint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the research planning module: the trained RL policy and experiment wrapper that generates one feasible motor design from requirement inputs inside the notebook/research environment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an integration-ready planning service: an API or packaged component that returns ranked design outputs and metadata for the sales quotation workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this project, everyone casually refers to the RL system as 'the planner,' so the phrase feels shared and natural; both think the other is simply endorsing the same workstream, and neither expects the distinction between research artifact and deployable component to need stating.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'validated' design set
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need 'validated results' before showing anything internally.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means aggregate evidence that the agent's proposals meet torque, current, and temperature constraints on the held-out evaluation suite using the lab's standard fast screening models.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means at least several specific recommended motor designs are checked through designer review or fresh high-fidelity simulation so users can inspect concrete trustworthy outputs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'validated results' sounds like ordinary quality language and does not invite clarification because both sides assume there is an obvious standard already established by prior project discussions.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the 'full simulator' run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the new batch should be run on the 'full simulator.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the established research training loop that combines analytical constraints, cached electromagnetic finite-element outcomes from earlier sweeps, and the surrogate thermal model to approximate full-design episodes quickly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means launching new end-to-end multiphysics evaluations for this sprint's sampled designs using the current simulation pipeline so there is no dependence on old caches.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Within the team, 'full simulator' is used informally to distinguish the richer loop from the toy environment, and both versions are considered more realistic than the toy setup; the wording therefore masks a major execution difference without sounding ambiguous.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the handoff will happen 'Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes Friday means an internal research handoff by end of day local time, with plots, checkpoints, and notes ready for the lab lead's review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes Friday means a same-day usable package, documentation, and endpoint or script checked into the shared repo early enough for the sales-tool team to begin trying it.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Deadlines are often stated as single days in fast-moving research meetings, and both participants presume the broader organizational context is already understood, so the operational meaning of 'handoff' remains unstated.

turns.inner_thought: I want to keep this sprint centered on a clean research story: retrain the RL policy, show stable held-out performance, and avoid getting dragged into a big deployment effort. When I say the planner, I mean the policy and the experiment wrapper we already use in the research environment. If we can align the next two weeks around that, the paper narrative stays intact.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I think the main goal for this sprint is to get the induction-motor RL planner ready for the internal demo and be clear on who owns what over the next two weeks.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we're finally talking about the planner as something the sales-tool side can actually try. If we can hand it off Friday in week two, with something callable and documented, that gives us immediate feedback on integration risk instead of another closed research cycle.
turns.utterance: Agreed. And if we can hand off the planner on Friday of the second week, the sales-tool side should be able to start trying it right away, which would be really useful.

turns.inner_thought: Before anything goes upward, I need one more batch and a compact evaluation package showing the policy is stable on the held-out requirement suite. Validated results, to me, means the screening numbers are solid and defensible in aggregate. That matters more for the paper than broad packaging work.
turns.utterance: My preference is that we focus first on one more training batch and a concise evaluation pack so we have validated results before we show anything internally.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, validated results are exactly what we need before anyone downstream trusts this. I want a few concrete customer-spec examples people can inspect, ideally the same kind of outputs they'd expect to see in a quotation flow. If there are specific cases everyone can look at, adoption conversations will go much more smoothly.
turns.utterance: Yes, definitely. Validated results are the minimum bar, and I think it would help if we also include a few representative customer-spec cases that people can inspect directly.

turns.inner_thought: I can kick off the standard full-simulator batch early this week in the research codebase—the hybrid loop with cached FE outcomes and the thermal surrogate. That should be fast enough to get reward curves and feasibility stats by Wednesday. No reason to reopen infrastructure questions for this sprint.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can launch the next batch on the full simulator early this week, and I should have updated reward curves and feasibility numbers by Wednesday.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect—fresh full-simulator outputs will give me the run artifacts I need for packaging, and if they're truly fresh from the current pipeline, that's much better for downstream confidence. I can tie those outputs to the planner package and reduce the chance that the sales-tool team hits basic trust issues immediately.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Fresh full-simulator outputs will also help on my side, because I can package the run artifacts together with the planner for downstream use.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep ownership of the actual science: retraining, screening analysis, plots, and selecting examples from the held-out set. Once the planner is stable in the research setup, Arjun can do a light wrap around it if needed. I really don't want to spend the sprint rebuilding interfaces when the main risk is still experimental quality.
turns.utterance: So from a work split perspective, I can take the policy retraining, the screening analysis, and the summary plots. Once the planner is stable, I'll pass it over for light wrapping.

turns.inner_thought: Great, if she's handing over the planner once it's stable, I can take care of turning it into something consumable: interface layer, formatting, docs, and enough structure that Friday is a real handoff. I need to make sure the repo and usage path are clean so the downstream team can start that same day.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll handle the interface layer, result formatting, and the repo documentation so the Friday handoff is smooth.

turns.inner_thought: For the internal report, I mostly need the numbers the lab lead will care about: success rates, pass counts, and a few examples from the screened set. That should be enough to support the claim that the agent is producing validated results without getting into time-consuming manual reviews.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—I can present those example outputs in the quotation-oriented shape the other team expects. If those are the validated cases, they should become the showcase examples in the planner package so people can judge whether this is usable in practice.
turns.utterance: That works. I'll prepare example outputs in the same format the quotation workflow expects, assuming the validated cases are the ones we'll showcase.

turns.inner_thought: Timeline-wise, I can share midweek checkpoints and have the policy, plots, and notes ready by Friday afternoon Munich time. That should be enough for internal review and to close the sprint cleanly. If Arjun wants to do a little wrapping after that, fine, but my deliverable is the research package.
